URI Faculty Senate Editorial Report October 15, 2026 Meeting Bill #2026-2027-IFSR-02 Approved by CBUM 10/8/26 Legislation Enacts Updates to Chapter 5 of the University Manual pertaining to the Public Safety Advisory Committee (PSAC) Proposal: The Senior Vice President for Administration and Finance/CFO’s office has offered the following updates to Section 5.47.13 to clarify terms and titles of various committee members.
The Constitution, By-Laws, and University Manual Committee (CBUM) met on 9/28/26 and affirmed that the proposal is editorial in nature and they agreed that relevant section of the manual should be amended.
They also offered a minor grammatical correction to the text which has been incorporated.
The Faculty Senate Executive Committee (FSEC) approved the proposal on 9/30/26.
Motion: No approval required.
The Senate is asked to accept the report as editorial.

Proposed Changes: 5.47.10 The Public Safety Advisory Committee is charged with advising and providing recommendations to the Department of Public Safety and its subunits, such as Transportation and Parking and Emergency Management, and to university leadership, at their request, regarding the programming and operational activities of the Department of Public Safety.
The PSAC is also charged with recommending administrative policies related to the Department of Public Safety broadly as well as to any of its subunits.
The Public Safety Advisory Committee may also review policies related to the Public Safety mission and its operations when requested to do so.
Administrative Report January 2024 5.47.11 The Public Safety Advisory Committee is not an internal review board and is not charged with the review of actions of individual members of the Public Safety staff, including police officers.
Administrative Report January 2024 5.47.12 The PSAC will meet quarterly, or more frequently upon the request of the President, the Committee chair, or the director of public safety.
Administrative 5.47.13 The PSAC Committee Chair shall be appointed by the President and serve a two-year term.

Membership may change over time, but generally shall include the Senior Vice President for Administration and Finance, the Vice President for Community, Equity and Diversity, the Assistant Associate Vice President of Facilities,

20260918 the Assistant Vice President, Housing and Residential Life and Student Development, Associate Vice President, Student Affairs and Campus Living, the Dean of Students, the Director Assistant Vice President of Public Safety and Chief of Police, the Deputy Chief of Police, and the Director of the Office of Equal Opportunity.
In addition, the committee will include three (3) faculty representatives nominated by the Faculty Senate Executive Committee (two-year term) , one (1) graduate student representative nominated by the Graduate Student Association (two-year term) , and one (1) undergraduate student representative nominated by the Student Senate (two-year term), and one (1) faculty or staff representative from each URI campus (appointed by and agreed upon by Provost and Vice President for Administration and Finance) (two-year term ).

FSEC (Faculty Senate Executive Committee) Meeting Minutes Date: Wednesday October 21, 2026 - Time: 10:00 am to 12:00 Pastore Hall Room 224 - Remote option via ZOOM Find the Acronym Glossary here Action Items: Staff will update the FSEC project/priority tracker based on recent legislative activity.
And staff will work with Pres.
Preisser to draft the agenda for the 11/19 FS meeting.
Staff will send the CoEd ‘Wednesday before Thanksgiving’ proposal to the Calendar Committee and CBUM for review and comment.
Staff will send the ‘Fannon Institute’ draft legislation to CBUM for review.
Pres.
Preisser will convey the FSEC’s preferred text to the Vice Provost regarding her ‘posthumous degree conferral’ bill.
Pres.
Preisser suggested that improvements to the dropdown menus in the required electronic forms for promotion/tenure/ESI’s could clear up misunderstandings about processes, and offered to talk to the relevant staff and report back to the FSEC and AAUP. 1.
Call to Order - Pres.
Preisser called the meeting to order at 10:03 am.
VP Trimm and Senators Van Wyk, Daniels, Meyerson, and Chen were present.
Past President Travis Williams was also on hand. 2.

Minutes for approval 2.1 Minutes of the 10/14/26 FSEC meeting.
The minutes were approved as edited. 3.
Priority Items and New Business 3.1.
Meeting Recap - 10/15/26 Faculty Senate Meeting - Regarding the land acknowledgment, it was agreed that flyers for community events addressed by the presenters should be incorporated into the slide deck for each meeting, but they would need to be received by staff in advance. 3.1.1 Status of Legislation: ● Course withdrawals legislation and back-up - The draft bill is being revised and will be back on the senate agenda for approval on Nov. 19.
The proposal will call for extending ‘at-will’ withdrawals through week 6 (versus week 3 as is the current limit) and during weeks 6 - 9, a dean’s signature will be required.
The Graduate School Dean has voiced an objection to changing the withdrawal period for graduate students.
Creating separate withdrawal calendars for undergraduate and graduate students is not the norm among peer institutions and FSEC is not in favor of this approach.
It is unclear if the entirety of the Graduate Council weighed in on the Dean’s position.
Pres.

Preisser will continue to liaise with the Graduate School in hopes of allaying their concerns and building support for the proposal. 3.1.2 Forum - College Liaisons - Incorporating feedback and next steps - FSEC members agreed the forum was managed well.
It was noted that there is some difficulty in making a strong ‘needs-based’ case for creating Liaisons while framing the issue in a positive light.
Opportunities to share best practices sets the right tone for a new committee, but there are serious governance challenges present in some colleges and faculty members would greatly benefit from the opportunity to share information with others who might be similarly situated.
It 1

was agreed that while not everyone sees the need, the idea should press forward and, even if the new Liaisons committee is not fully populated at the outset, it might gain traction once formed.
Ideally, the committee would be effective and gain full representation over time.
An alternative was discussed in case the senate is unable to fully populate an entirely new committee from current apportionment.
This would involve rolling the liaison duties into the charge of an existing committee.
FSEC agreed to continue the conversation next week. 3.2.
Current Project Tracker and Advance Agenda Setting updates - Staff will update the tracker based on recent legislative activity.
The FS President will work with staff to refine draft agendas for the next couple of FS meetings. 3.3.
Committee Assignment Updates - Assignments are nearly complete, but there will be one or two more appointments pending in November. 3.4.
Advance Planning for the November 19 FS meeting - including compensation forum - The draft agenda was briefly reviewed.
The bulk of the discussion centered around the planned senate service compensation forum.
Pres.

Preisser presented slides which will be part of that presentation and discussion.
A number of suggestions were made, including reordering the slides: the graphs showing the widening margin between senate compensation rates and faculty compensation rates overall should be preceded by information on how (and how much) the senate workload has increased.
Pres.
Preisser hopes to finalize the slides soon so they can be shared with the administration as a courtesy, well before the 11/19 meeting.
FSEC members stressed that while increased compensation is a desired outcome, another goal, which should be attended to as part of the forum, would be providing clarity around the compensation model.
For example, most senators don’t seem to know which members of the leadership team are eligible for ‘stipends’ or release from normal duties as part of their Executive Committee or other Committee chair service.
Examples (anonymized) can be provided of how the various deans treat senate service and there needs to be some standardization and predictability.
In recent years, senate officers have often not been granted course release by their deans, which makes monetary compensation even more important.

It must also be made clear that compensation for service through faculty development funds (rather than funds that can be taken as pay) is not effective and this practice should be discouraged. 3.5.
Guidance for the newly formed Nominating Committee - FSEC members were asked to start thinking about senators who might make good FSEC members next year and to also consider running for the VP position.
The nominating committee would like an initial list to work from as they begin their outreach. 4.
Continued Items 4.1.
Faculty Concerns submitted through the FS Webpage - Three new concerns had been submitted.
Two were related and pertained to lack of availability of office and lab space for faculty (computer science department, in particular).
It was agreed that Pres.
Preisser will speak to the relevant Dean in hopes of finding a solution.
The third concern identified a typo in FSEC meeting minutes, which will be corrected. 4.2.
Ongoing Discussion - Creation of a Programs Subcommittee (current draft) - VP Trimm has transmitted a proposal to CBUM and CASC and will report back once he receives their feedback and reactions. 2

4.3.
College of Education concern related to using the Wednesday before Thanksgiving as a class day when needed.
The College of Education drafted a formal proposal that would include the Wednesday before Thanksgiving as a class day in exceptional circumstances in lieu of using Columbus Day/Indigenous People’s Day.
The proposal stems from the fact that the university has made an intentional effort to acknowledge the indigenous people of the area and their culture, and failing to honor the holiday detracts from that.
CoEd faculty also noted the operational and logistical problems posed by holding classes when most offices on campus are closed, making certain student-facing services unavailable.
FSEC members agreed the issue is worthy of senate consideration and approved the proposal.
It will be sent to the Calendar Committee and CBUM for review and comment. 5.
Updates/Ongoing Items 5.1.
Updates - Meetings with Administrators, Committees, or Others 5.1.1 Other Updates - Budget; College level governance concerns, etc.
FSEC members were briefed on a college-level governance issue ongoing in CHS which stands to affect curricular approval processes. 6.

New Business – Open for additional items not listed in the agenda. 7.1 UM amendments related to University College/Fannon Institute transition - Director for Academic Advising Services Cindie Cruger had submitted updates to Chapters 3 and 8 of the Manual, which are related to the transition from the old University College for Academic Success to the Fannon Institute for Student Success.
FSEC did not see anything problematic in the language at a glance, but agreed it deserved a closer read.
It will remain on next week’s agenda.
In the meantime, staff should send the draft to CBUM for review and comment, in hopes of docketing the bill on the 11/19 FS agenda. 7.2 Consideration of Posthumous Degree conferral changes (UM Chp. 8) - The Vice Provost had provided a draft of amendments to Section 8.22.50 of the UM dealing with posthumous degrees.
The amendment would allow the ‘50% completion toward degree requirements’ clause to be waived.
FSEC discussed the matter at length, weighing the importance of the so-called 50% requirement and how it could be refined and/or interpreted.

Ultimately, it was decided that, since the requirement can be waived in certain circumstances, there would seem to be no harm in removing the requirement altogether, and leaving the decision to the discretion of the department chair, dean, and university president.
Pres.
Preisser will convey the FSEC’s preferred text to theVice Provost. 7.3 Review Process for ESI Requests (esp. vis a vis AAUP contract) - Sen.
Van Wyk informed FSEC of her communication with the AAUP director who opined conclusively that ESI’s are not to be treated like annual reviews and fellow faculty should not be part of any peer review of these requests.
Any peer reviews initiated were the result of a mis-read by the chair or dean and should not be completed.
Correspondence to that effect will be sent from the AAUP to the affected department(s).
Pres.
Preisser opined that improvements to the dropdown menus in the required electronic forms could probably clear this up.

He will talk to the relevant staff and report back to the FSEC and AAUP. 7.4 The uncompensated service burden of senior faculty (LM) - This was briefly discussed at the last meeting and it was noted it would be most appropriate for the SCLC to explore the issue and make recommendations.
Sen.
Van Wyk is liaison to the SCLC and will ask that they focus some 3

effort here. Pres. Preisser stressed the importance of proposing a tangible action item or outcome for the senate. 7. Closing Remarks – Recap of decisions made, action items, and plans for the next meeting. It was noted that incidents like those in the news about Cornell University lately are troubling for everyone involved in higher education. It was wondered if there was anything preventative that the faculty can do via the faculty senate. Staff was asked to place an item on next week’s agenda for discussion/brainstorming. 8. Adjournment - The meeting adjourned at 11:45 am. 4

Article III, Section 7 – Ethical conduct. The people of the State of Rhode Island believe that public officials and employees must adhere to the highest standards of ethical conduct, respect the public trust and the rights of all persons, be open, accountable and responsive, avoid the appearance of impropriety and not use their position for private gain or advantage.
WHAT IS “ETHICAL” CONDUCT?

Ethics: a standard or philosophy of right and wrong human behavior based on logical reasoning So… “Ethical Conduct” is the type of behavior that a logical person would agree is the “right” thing to do under the circumstances But - People have different ideas about what makes behavior “right” or “wrong”
Ethics based on CULTURE – Many people think that whether something is “ethical” depends on the setting in which it occurs, taking into account the local culture, habits and customs.

Ethics based on CONSEQUENCES - Ethical or unethical conduct is determined by examining the results. Ethical conduct is behavior that results in more positive results than negative results, in quantity and quality.

Ethics based on CHARACTER - Ethical conduct is determined by asking, “What would a virtuous person do under the circumstances?” The focus is on one’s character and motives. I am an honest, upstanding person, so how could I violate the Code of Ethics?

Focus on your ACTION, not the result ! ! ! The Code of Ethics tells us what actions to avoid, without regard to culture, consequence, or character. Ethical or unethical conduct is determined NOT by looking at the results, but at the conduct itself and judging its inherent rightness or wrongness.
Who is subject to the Code of Ethics? All elected and appointed officials and employees of state and local government, boards, commissions and agencies shall be subject to the Code of Ethics.

A person subject to the Code of Ethics . . . may not participate in any matter in which he or she has an interest, financial or otherwise, which is in substantial conflict with the proper discharge of his or her duties in the public interest. A substantial conflict of interest occurs if it is reasonably foreseeable that he or she or any family member or business associate, or any business by which he or she is employed or represents, will derive a direct monetary gain or suffer a direct monetary loss by reason of his or her official activity.

Reasonably foreseeable The conflict need not be certain to occur, but the probability must be greater than “conceivably.” Business Associates Your “business associates” are any persons or entities that you are joined with to achieve a common financial objective. These include not only your business partners, but also people you have hired such as an attorney, accountant, realtor, contractor, etc. These also include any businesses or organizations, even if not-for-profit, for which you are an officer or serve on the Board of Directors.

A conflict of interest is a situation where a person’s public duties impact, or involve, his or her private life. ► It is not unethical to have a conflict of interest. ► It does not violate the Code of Ethics to have a conflict of interest. ► It is not the conflict that is the problem; rather, the potential problem is in a failure to identify and manage the conflict.

Do I have a conflict of interest? Ask yourself . . . Is it “reasonably foreseeable” that: A decision I am helping to make as part of my public duties, will result in a financial benefit or detriment to: Me; or My family or household member; or My outside employer; or My business associate?

Ask yourself: Even if there is no financial impact, is a family member, household member, employer or business associate a party to, or participating in, the matter being discussed? If the answer is “Yes,” then you have a conflict of interest and you must recuse from any participation in the matter.

HOW TO RECUSE 1. Complete a Statement of Conflict of Interest form. 2. Present the original to your presiding officer, appointing authority, director, or immediate supervisor. 3. Send a copy to the Ethics Commission.

Nepotism - You may not participate in any matter as part of your public duties if there is reason to believe or expect that any person within your family or a household member . . . • is a party to or participant in such matter; or • will derive a direct monetary gain; or • will suffer a direct monetary loss; or • obtain an employment advantage.

These prohibitions apply regardless of whether a family or household member is objectively the most qualified candidate for a job, or is deserving of promotion. The policy underlying the prohibitions against nepotism in the Code recognizes that it is difficult for any person to be truly objective when considering matters impacting family/household members and, additionally, furthers the constitutionally founded goal of avoiding the appearance of impropriety.

Scenario – Andy is a member of the Anytown Town Council. The Town has just released a Request for Proposals (RFP) for the construction of a municipal playground. Billy is Andy’s nephew. Billy’s construction company submits a bid in response to the RFP.
RHODE ISLAND STATEOf HOPE Andy must recuse from all aspects of the bid selection process.
Advocacy/Supervision – You may not participate in the supervision, evaluation, appointment, classification, promotion, transfer, or discipline of any person in your family or a household member.

Advocacy/Supervision – You may not delegate to a subordinate any tasks relating to the supervision, evaluation, appointment, classification, promotion, transfer, or discipline of any person in your family or household member.

Budgets– You may not participate in discussions or decision-making regarding a budgetary line item that would address or affect the employment, compensation, or benefits of any person in your family or a household member.

Budgets– You may participate in discussion and decision-making relative to approving or rejecting an entire budget as a whole - provided . . . the person within your family or household member is impacted by the entire budget as a member of a significant and definable class of persons, and not individually or to any greater extent than any other similarly situated member of the class.

Collective Bargaining/Employment Contracts– You may not participate in negotiations relative to an employee contract or collective bargaining which addresses or affects the employment, compensation, or benefits of any person in your family or a household member.

Collective Bargaining/Employment Contracts– You may participate in a decision to accept or reject an entire employee contract or collective bargaining agreement as a whole - provided . . . the person within your family or household member is impacted by the entire contract or agreement as a member of a significant and definable class of persons, and not individually or to any greater extent than any other similarly situated member of the class.

► Recusal is not the same as abstaining, which may mean that the public official will not vote, but has participated in discussions on a matter. ► Recusal means that you are not participating in deliberations or debates, making recommendations, giving advice, considering findings, or in any other way assuming responsibility for or participating in any aspect of the work or decision-making relating to the matter where there are potential conflicts of interest.

Recusal does not mean that the public official must leave the room if it is an open meeting, although it is best practice to do so. However, if the public body is in executive session, once the official has recused, he or she has no more right to be in the room than any other member of the general public.

No person subject to the Code of Ethics may enter into any contract with a state or municipal agency unless . . . the contract has been awarded through an open and public process, including prior public notice and subsequent public disclosure of all proposals considered and contracts awarded.

Contracts for professional services which have been customarily awarded without competitive bidding shall not be subject to competitive bidding if awarded through a process of public notice and disclosure of financial details.

STATE VENDORS PROVIDING GOODS OR SERVICES TO PUBLIC OFFICIALS

No state vendor shall provide goods or services for less than fair market value for the personal use of a procurement official of a state agency – if – the vendor has sold goods and services during the preceding twenty-four (24) months to the state agency – or – if the vendor knows or has reason to know he or she will be submitting a bid or making a proposal for the sale of goods or services within the succeeding twenty-four (24) months to the state agency.

No procurement official of a state agency shall accept goods or services for his or her personal use for less than the fair market value from a state vendor who has sold goods or services to the agency during the preceding twenty-four (24) months – or – who the procurement official knows or has reason to know will be submitting a bid or making a proposal for the sale of goods or services to the agency within the succeeding twenty-four (24) months.

Secondary Employment You may have a private or public sector job in addition to your state/municipal position; however, you may not accept outside employment that impairs your independence of judgment or that induces you to disclose confidential government information.

When considering potential conflicts of interest regarding secondary employment, the Commission examines a number of factors: • nexus between public duties & private employment • whether such work is completed outside normal work hours & without use of public resources • whether the official/employee would appear before own agency • whether such work would be conducted outside of areas over which official/employee has decision-making jurisdiction • whether official/employee would use his or her public position to solicit business or customers

The Appearance of Impropriety The appearance of impropriety is a phrase referring to a situation which to a layperson without knowledge of the specific circumstances might seem to raise ethics questions.

The Appearance of Impropriety When enacting the Code of Ethics, the General Assembly included as one of its legislative purposes the elimination of impropriety. The legislature did not, however, make the appearance of impropriety a violation of the law.

WHAT IS AN ADVISORY OPINION? An advisory opinion is a legal interpretation of the Rhode Island Code of Ethics issued by the Ethics Commission which provides specific guidance about a particular and impending circumstance. Advisory opinions are based upon the representations made by, or on behalf of, the persons or entities requesting them, and are not the result of adversarial or investigative proceedings.
